title: Which pattern is behind dependency injection?
summary: Checks that you understand DI isn't magic — a container running a Factory for you.

slides.markdown:
"Which pattern is behind dependency injection?" checks whether you understand DI as a mechanism built from familiar pieces, rather than framework magic. The honest answer: DI itself is a *technique* (Dependency Inversion applied at object-construction time), and the pattern doing the actual work underneath a DI container is a Factory — the container is essentially a large, configuration-driven Factory building an object graph.

Getting this right shows you can see through a framework's abstraction to the plain mechanism underneath.

slides.sectionTitle: Clarifying question: the container's internals, or the pattern DI itself embodies?
slides.markdown:
Ask which layer they want. "How [DI](dependency-injection-and-testability) helps testability" is about the technique's benefit — swapping real dependencies for test doubles. "Which pattern is behind it" is about mechanism — what's actually happening inside `new ApplicationContext()` when it wires up your objects.

This question is specifically the second one, so lead with the mechanism (Factory) rather than restating DI's testability benefits, which is a different, more commonly-asked question.

slides.sectionTitle: The answer skeleton: DI is Dependency Inversion applied via a Factory (or Abstract Factory) the container runs for you
slides.markdown:
DI is Dependency Inversion (a design principle: depend on abstractions, not concretions) applied via a [Factory](factory-method-and-abstract-factory) — or an Abstract Factory, for a whole family of related dependencies — that the container runs on your behalf. When a container resolves `PaymentService`'s constructor and sees it needs a `PaymentGateway`, it's doing exactly what a hand-written factory method would do: deciding which concrete class to construct and supplying it.

The container's value-add isn't a new pattern — it's automating a Factory across your entire object graph instead of writing one by hand per class.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: "is Service Locator the same thing?" — no, and here's the difference that matters
slides.markdown:
No, and the difference is the direction of control. With DI, the container **pushes** dependencies into a class through its constructor — the class never asks for anything. With Service Locator, the class **pulls** its dependency by calling out to a global registry from inside its own code, which means the dependency is invisible from the constructor and only discoverable by reading the method body.

"Push vs pull" is the one-sentence version of the difference, and it's the reason DI is considered the better default despite both solving "how do I get an instance of X."

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: "why does Service Locator make unit testing harder than constructor injection?"
slides.markdown: With constructor injection, a test can pass a mock `PaymentGateway` directly into `PaymentService`'s constructor — no global state involved. With Service Locator, the test has to first configure the global `ServiceLocator` registry with a mock before running the code under test, and reset it afterward to avoid leaking that mock into other tests — turning every test into stateful setup and teardown around a shared global, instead of a plain constructor call.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: "what pattern handles object lifetime — singleton vs per-request scope — inside the container?"
slides.markdown:
The container's own **scope** mechanism, which is really a specialized Singleton (or a pool of them, one per scope instance) managed by the container instead of hand-rolled by each class. Registering a bean as `singleton`-scoped means the container constructs it once and hands out the same instance to every dependent — exactly the one-instance guarantee Singleton provides, but without any of Singleton's usual testability problems, since the container can substitute a different instance in tests without touching production code.

`request`- or `prototype`-scoped beans just mean the container's internal Factory runs again per scope instead of once — no new pattern, just a parameter on the same mechanism.

slides.sectionTitle: Weak answer: "DI is a pattern" — DI is a technique; the container's mechanism is what implements a pattern
slides.markdown:
**Weak belief:** "DI is a pattern."

**Why it's weak:** DI is a *technique* — a way of supplying dependencies from outside rather than constructing them internally — not itself one of the GoF patterns. Calling it "a pattern" without qualification misses the actual question, which is asking what pattern *implements* the technique underneath.

**Correct model:** say "DI is a technique; the container implementing it typically runs a Factory (or Abstract Factory) to build the object graph" — naming both the technique and its underlying mechanism is what the question is actually checking for.

slides.sectionTitle: Wrong answer: conflating Service Locator (pull) with Dependency Injection (push) as the same approach
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** treating Service Locator and Dependency Injection as basically the same approach because "both give you an instance of the dependency you need."

**Why it's wrong:** the direction of control is fundamentally different — DI pushes dependencies in through the constructor, keeping them visible and declared; Service Locator pulls them from inside the method body via a global lookup, hiding them from anything reading the class's public interface. Treating them as interchangeable misses the exact problem DI was designed to solve.

**Correct model:** always distinguish push (DI, visible, preferred) from pull (Service Locator, hidden, generally discouraged) rather than grouping them by their shared surface-level goal.

DI is Dependency Inversion applied via a Factory (or Abstract Factory) the container runs for you — the container isn't a new pattern, it's a Factory automated across your whole object graph. Service Locator looks similar but pulls a dependency from a global registry inside a method body instead of the container pushing it through the constructor, which is what makes it harder to test and less visible.

Object lifetime (singleton vs per-request scope) inside the container is a specialized, container-managed Singleton — again, not a new pattern, just the same mechanism running under container control instead of hand-rolled per class.
